previous.passage: We called it the salt pool, though by Bartolo's ninth summer in Havana the sea had long since cracked its seaward wall. Each morning Dario sat on the edge with his trousers rolled and named things for her in the old language: tile, gull, the green rust on the ladder. She repeated each word and swam a length between words. On Thursday she stopped halfway, clung to the rope, and climbed out by the near ladder, saying the water was too cold. Dario, who had seen everything, said only that cold had two words, one for water and one for people, and made her practice both. She did not tell him she had wanted to reach the far wall before her mother arrived. He did not tell her he had noticed. When they walked home, she carried his towel, and he carried the word for rope, saying it over to himself.

previous.passage: “Walk me to the railing, if you are not too tired,” Ofelia said, though the doctor had forbidden the night air. I wheeled her along the promenade at Valparaiso, as I had each evening that month, and she counted the lamps aloud, as she always did, never once losing the number. That afternoon I had found, among her blankets, a letter addressed to her son in Santiago, unsealed and plainly unfinished. When I mentioned that the post left at dawn, she asked whether the gulls ever slept, and whether I had a son myself. At the railing she held out the letter and asked me to read it to her, slowly, every line. I read it. She corrected two words, made me read it again, and then folded it into my apron pocket and turned her chair, without my help, toward the lamps.
previous.question: Based on the passage, why does Ofelia most likely ask the narrator to read the letter aloud?
options: She doubts her own memory and needs help recalling what she wrote
She wishes to keep the letter's contents secret from her son
She wants the letter sent but cannot bear to send it by herself
She is testing whether the nurse has already read her private letter

previous.passage: Haruto has already taken the better chair when you arrive at the tailor's back room in Addis Ababa, so you take the stool by the bolts of cotton and say good morning as if you meant it. You and he have baked on the same street for nine years. The rule, written by no one, is that neither of you sells bread before seven; the market council has called you both to decide whether it still holds now that the bus station has moved. Lindiwe, the tailor, pours tea and leaves you to it. Haruto compliments your new ovens. You compliment his sign. He stirs his tea long after the sugar has gone, and you count the pins in the cushion beside you: forty, forty-one. When the clerk finally arrives, the two of you rise at the same moment, and each holds the curtain open for the other until it slips from both your hands.

previous.passage: When Weiqi climbed up to the roof the first evening back, I was already sitting against the water tank, pretending to read. Taipei hummed below us, scooters and rain on tin, and she said the view had not changed, which was untrue; three new towers stood where the night market had been. I said it was nice of her to visit. “Yuxuan, I didn't visit,” she said. “I moved back.” For a while we talked about her new school, the price of mangoes, my brother's motorbike, and I laughed at the right places.
